Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 1:

Surat al-Fajr

It is Meccan according to the majority opinion. ʿAli ibn Abi Talha said: it is Madani. Its verses number thirty-two according to the Hijazi reckoning, thirty according to the Kufi and Syrian reckoning, and twenty-nine according to the Basri reckoning. When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in the surah before it, ﴿Faces that Day will be downcast﴾ and ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful﴾, He followed it with mention of the groups of arrogant deniers whose faces are downcast. He, majestic is His glory, alluded to the other category, whose faces are joyful, by His saying in this surah: ﴿O soul at rest﴾. Also, in it there is what relates to the matter of al-Ghashiya (the Overwhelming) and what is in it.

The Jalal al-Suyuti said: The connection (of this surah with the previous one) has not become clear to me in any aspect except that its beginning is like an oath confirming the truth of what the previous surah ended with, or confirming what it contains of promise and threat. This is in addition to the fact that the sentence ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt﴾ resembles the sentence ﴿Do they not look﴾, and this is as you see.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the dawn﴾. Allah, glorified is He, swore by the dawn, just as He, mighty and majestic, swore by the morning in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And by the morning when it breathes﴾. So what is meant by it is the well-known dawn, as narrated from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr, and others, may Allah be pleased with them.

It was said: what is meant is its column (of light) and its extended illumination. Its origin is splitting a thing with a wide cleft, and the morning was named fajr (dawn) because it splits (fajara) the night. There are two kinds: the false dawn, which is not bound by the rulings of fasting and prayer, and the true dawn, to which their rulings are bound. Scholars have spoken at length about the reason for each, and some of it has already passed. Perhaps what is meant here is the true dawn, as it is more fitting for an oath. According to many, what is meant is the category of dawn, not the dawn of a specific day.

From Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid: the dawn of the day of sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). From ʿIkrima: the dawn of Friday. From al-Dahhak: the dawn of Dhu al-Hijja. From Muqatil: the dawn of the night of Jamʿ (Muzdalifa).

Saʿid ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it is the dawn of Muharram, the dawn of the year. A similar report is narrated from Qatada. And from the same scholar (al-Habr, i.e. Ibn ʿAbbas) also: that it is the whole day. Ibn Jarir narrated from him also that he said: it means the dawn prayer (Salat al-Fajr). A similar report is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam. So it is either by supposing an omitted idafa (construct phrase), or by applying the term to the prayer figuratively, which is common.

It was said: what is meant is the bursting forth of springs from rocks and other things.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 2:

﴿And by the ten nights﴾. They are the first ten [days] of Dhu al-Hijjah (the first ten days of al-Adha), as al-Hakim narrated and authenticated, and a group [of scholars] [narrated it] from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also reported from Ibn al-Zubayr, Masruq, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and others.

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman also narrated this from Jabir, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and these [nights] have such merit as they have.

Ahmad and al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and more excellent than the days of these ten." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, not even jihad in the way of Allah?" He said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah, except for a man who strives in the way of Allah with his self and his wealth and returns with nothing of that."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the last ten [nights] of Ramadan. It is also reported from al-Dahhak. Indeed, al-Tabrizi claimed a consensus that they are these ten [days] and that no one differed concerning it, and some [scholars] cited as evidence for it the hadith agreed upon as authentic.

'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "When the ten [nights] began — meaning the last ten [nights] of Ramadan — the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would tighten his waist-wrapper, enliven his night, and wake his family."

Some [scholars] objected to this, saying that it is possible that this was [done] so that he (ﷺ) might attain the Night of Decree, because it falls within them, and not because they are the ten intended here. From Ibn Jurayj [it is reported] that they are the first ten [nights] of Ramadan, and from Yamani and a group [it is reported] that they are the first ten [days] of Muharram, in which is the Day of 'Ashura', and much has been related about its merit.

Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah while the Jews were fasting on the Day of 'Ashura'. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'What is this day that you fast?' They said: 'It is a great day, on which Allah saved Musa and drowned the family of Pharaoh. Musa, peace be upon him, fasted it out of gratitude.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'We have more right to Musa than you.' So he (ﷺ) fasted it and commanded [the Muslims] to fast it."

It is established in the two Sahihs that "on the morning of 'Ashura', he (ﷺ) sent [a message] to the villages of the Ansar around Madinah: 'Whoever has woken up fasting should complete his day, and whoever has woken up not fasting should fast the rest of his day.'" So the Companions afterwards would fast it and have their small children fast it too, and they would take them to the mosque and make for them toys of wool; when one of them cried for food, they would give him the toy until it was time to break the fast.

Ahmad and others narrated from the Habr (scholar) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Fast the Day of 'Ashura', and differ from the Jews in it, and fast a day before it and a day after it."

Concerning the command to be generous to one's dependents on it, several weak hadiths have come. But al-Bayhaqi said: "Even though they are weak, when some of them are combined with others they become stronger." In any case, their indefiniteness [in the verse, ﴿ولَيالٍ﴾] is for magnification, and the word "qul" [in the sense of "some"] is for partiality, because they are some of the nights of the year or of the month, and magnification is more fitting. It was said: Were it not for the intention of what has been mentioned, the apparent [form] would be to define them like their counterparts, because they are known, specific nights. Some [scholars] estimated, to make the prayer of Fajr intended in what passed, a noun to be supplied here: i.e., "and the worship of nights." And something similar is said of what follows, according to some of the views on it, but it is not necessary and has no effect on it. Ibn 'Abbas read it with the construct form, so some [readers] vocalized it: ﴿ولَيالٍ عَشْرٍ﴾ with the tanwin and without a ya', and some [read] "wa-layali 'ashr" with the ya', which is the analogical form. The intended meaning is "wa-layali ayyam 'ashr" (and nights of ten days), so the qualified noun, which is the counted item, has been omitted; and in such a construction the feminine ta' may or may not be used with the numeral. From this is: "and he followed it with six [days] of Shawwal," and what al-Kisa'i related, "five of the month" as an implicit [expression]. The preference for omitting it here is that it occurs as a closing rhyme (fasilah). It was also permitted that the construct be explanatory (bayaniyyah), but this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 3:

﴿By the even and the odd﴾. They are, according to the marfu' hadith of Jabir which we pointed to earlier, the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr) and the Day of 'Arafah.

Al-Tibi said: We have related from Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, from Imran ibn Husayn, that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the even and the odd, and he said: 'The prayer, some of it is even and some of it is odd.'" Then he said: "This is the interpretation from which there is no escape." End of quotation. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Abi Hatim also related it from Imran, and Ibn Abi Hatim declared it sound. However, in al-Bahr it is stated that the hadith of Jabir has a stronger chain than the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn. Beyond this there are many other opinions. 'Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Hasan that he said: "Our Lord swore by the whole number, of which some is even and some is odd." 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Mujahid that he said: "All creation is even and odd, so He swore by His creation." 

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from him that he said: "Allah is the Odd (al-Witr), and His creation is the Even (al-Shaf'); the male and the female." Something similar is reported from Abu Salih and Masruq, and they recited: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾. It was also said: the intended meaning is the even and odd of those nights. It was said: the even is the days of 'Ad and the odd is their nights. It was said: the even is the gates of Paradise and the odd is the gates of Hell. Other things have also been said. In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, thirty-six opinions are mentioned regarding them. In al-Kashshaf: "They have gone to great lengths regarding the even and the odd, until they nearly exhausted the kinds of things they may refer to, and that is of little benefit and deserves to be neglected."

One of the scholars said: The words "even" and "odd" do not indicate the specification of anything from what they mentioned, nor its determination. Rather, they only indicate a general meaning that encompasses all of that. Perhaps whoever interpreted them with what he interpreted them did not claim that the meaning is restricted to what he explained, but singled out for mention from among the types of their referents what he saw as more evident in indicating Oneness, or more relevant to the religion, or more fitting to what precedes or follows, or more beneficial and requiring gratitude, or similar subtleties. And if it is established from the Lawgiver (upon him be prayer and peace) that he explained them in some aspects, the apparent meaning is that it was not based on restricting the referent, but came by way of illustration, with the view that singling it out for mention carried a valuable benefit. In that case, it is permissible for the exegete to take the word to some other of its possible meanings for another benefit. End of quotation.

This is an inclination to the view that the definite article (al) in both words is generic (li'l-jins) and not for a specific reference (li'l-'ahd). The apparent position is that the two hadiths mentioned above are an instance of definitive specification and not illustration, but the reconciliation between them then becomes problematic. If what al-Bahr says is correct, then the hadith of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) is the one to rely on. And Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Aghharr from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', Ibn Waththab, Qatadah, Talhah, al-A'mash, and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read: "wal-Iwtri" (وِالوِتْرِ) with a kasrah on the waw, which is the dialect of Tamim. The majority read it with a fathah, which is the dialect of Quraysh. Both are dialects, like "al-habr" and "al-hibr" meaning scholar, as the author of al-Matla' said regarding al-witr meaning the opposite of the even. As for "al-Iwtri" meaning vengeance or enmity (tirah), only the kasrah is heard for it, and al-Asma'i also related both dialects for it. Yunus, from Abu 'Amr, read with a fathah on the waw and a kasrah on the ta', and this is either a dialect or the transfer of the vowel of the waw to the preceding letter in pause.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 4:

﴿By the night when it passes on﴾. That is, it goes on, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the night when it turns its back﴾ and ﴿By the night when it dark-falls﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) or a metaphor (isti'arah), the aspect of resemblance being like the day. And "idha" (when), as the scholar al-Taftazani clearly stated in al-Talwih, is a substitute (badal) for (al-layl) [the night], and its departure from the sense of a temporal adverb is not objectionable. Or it is an adverb of time connected to an elided noun (mudaf muqaddar), namely "al-azamah" (greatness), as some of them have chosen. The oath by that time, or restricting the greatness to it, is due to what it contains of clear indication of perfect power and abundant blessing. Or the verb "yasri" is used in it, as Abu Hayyan reported from al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah, like their saying: "salla al-maqam" (the station was prayed), meaning: it was prayed at it, the attribution being metonymically transferred, ascribing to time what is properly ascribed to place. Whichever of these is the case, the intended meaning of "al-layl" is its genus. Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: what is meant by it is the night of sacrifice (laylat al-nahr), in which pilgrims travel at night to Muzdalifah after departing from Arafat. But this is not so. The oath and the restriction on the last interpretation are due to what there is in travelling at night of the blessing of protection from the heat of the sun and the evil of highway robbers, generally.

The letter "ya'" is omitted from the end of ﴿yasri﴾ according to the majority, both in continuation and in pausing, although it is the lam of an imperfect verb that is not jussive, being satisfied with the kasrah in its place for lightness and so that the verse-endings (ru'us al-ay) agree. That is why it is written so in the mushafs. It should not be said that it was omitted because it is dropped in its written form, for that implies that the recitation follows the orthography without a prior transmission, and this is not correct. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr in one transmission restricted this omission to pausing, for the sake of observing the endings, while Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub did not omit it at all.

In the tafsir of al-Baghawi: al-Akhfash was asked about the reason for the dropping of the "ya'" of ﴿yasri﴾, and he said: "The night does not travel, but travel is made in it." This is an explanation that is often questioned for its obscurity, and the answer is that he meant that when the expression was turned away from the apparent sense in meaning and other things, its due was to be a meaning other than its wording, because a thing draws its kind to it through familiarity with it: "Birds fall upon their like." This is like what has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾, that when it was turned away from "baghiyah" (an unchaste woman), the "ta'" was dropped from it and it was not said "baghiyyah." This is among the marvels of the Arabic language. It is also possible to give the reason in a similar way when ﴿yasri﴾ is interpreted as "yamdi" (passes on), because in it there is also a turning away from the apparent sense in meaning, which is known from the fact that it is a metaphor in that.

Abu al-Dinar al-A'rabi read "al-fajri", "al-watri" and "yasri" with tanwin in all three. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is like what is related from some Arabs, that they paused on the ends of rhyming lines with tanwin, even if they were verbs or had "al" in them, such as his saying:

"Cease your blame, O my censurer, and the reproach,
And say, if I am hit, indeed it has hit me."

End.

This is as Abu Hayyan said: the grammarians mentioned it in the unrestricted rhymes (al-qawafi al-mutlaqah), meaning those with a vowel, when the poet does not chant. It is one of two modes of the Arabs when they do not chant. The other mode is pausing, so they say "al-'itab" and "asab," as they do when they pause on a word in prose. This A'rabi treated the verse-endings as if they were in pause and dealt with them as unrestricted rhymes. This tanwin is called tanwin al-tarannum (the tanwin of chanting), and it is not specific to nouns. It is my strong impression that it was said to be written as a nun, unlike the kinds of tanwin specific to nouns.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is there in that﴾ and so on, is a confirmation and affirmation of the grandeur of the things mentioned in the oath, and that they deserve to be magnified by being sworn by. It thereby indicates the magnification and emphasis of what is sworn to, by way of allusion (kinayah). So "that" (dhalika) refers to the thing sworn by, and the sense of distance in it serves to increase its magnification. That is: is there, among the things mentioned, ﴿an oath﴾, i.e., something sworn by, ﴿for one of understanding (dhi hijr)﴾, i.e., would it be fitting in his view to swear by it out of reverence and magnification? The intended meaning is to confirm that all of them are such. This mode of expression was chosen to emphasize the truth and to signal that the matter is evident. It is like a speaker who, after citing a proof whose indication is clear regarding his claim, says: "Does this not prove what we have said?" It is also permissible that the confirmation is that people of understanding (dhawu al-hijr) affirm with the like of that which is sworn to, so that it likewise indicates its magnification and emphasis. In that case, "that" refers to the verbal noun, namely the oath: is there, in my swearing by those things, an oath acceptable to a person of understanding, which he counts as valid, which he does in like manner, and by which he affirms what is sworn to? The outcome of the two views regarding the affirmation of what is sworn to is one, although the manner differs, as is not hidden. The first is perhaps more apparent. Al-hijr (intellect, reason) means that it restrains its possessor (yahjuru sahibahu), i.e., prevents him from falling into what is not fitting, just as it is called ʿaql (intellect) and nuhyah (discernment) because it understands (yaʿqilu) and forbids (yanha), and ḥaṣāh (reason/sense) from al-ihsa', which is control. Al-Farra' said: It is said of someone that he is dhu hijr when he restrains himself and keeps himself in control. The thing sworn to is omitted; it is: ﴿He will surely be punished﴾, as is indicated by His saying, Exalted is His majesty:

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?﴾ etc. This is an appeal to the knowledge of the Prophet (ﷺ) through what shows the punishment of ʿĀd and their likes, who shared with his people, upon him be peace, in transgression and corruption. It follows the pattern of: ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Ibrahim (Abraham) about his Lord?﴾ etc. And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾

Abu Hayyan said: What appears is that it is omitted, indicated by what precedes it from the end of the surah, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ ﴿then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾. Its estimate is: their return is to Us and their reckoning is upon Us.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited: ﴿By the dawn﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿when it passes﴾, and he said: "This is an oath that your Lord is indeed in ambush." Ibn al-Anbari went to the view that this is the thing sworn to (muqsam ʿalayhi). And from Muqatil that he said: "Is there in that..." etc., and "hal" (هل, "is there") here has the meaning of "inna" (إنّ, "indeed"). This is false both in transmission and in reason, since then there would remain an oath without a thing sworn to.

The intended ʿĀd is the descendants of ʿĀd ibn ʿAws ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh (Noah), upon him be peace, the people of Hud, upon him be peace. They were named after their father, just as the Banu Hashim were named after Hashim. The use of "father" for his offspring is a common metaphor (majaz), to the extent that some of it has been assimilated to the literal sense. It has been said that their earliest were called "the first ʿĀd" and their latest "the last ʿĀd."

ʿImad al-Din Ibn Kathir said: Whenever the report of ʿĀd occurs in the Qur'an, the ʿĀd meant in it is the first ʿĀd, except in Surat al-Ahqaf. They are also called Iram, naming them after their grandfather, and naming by the grandfather is also common. Iram is a term specific to the first (ʿĀd). On this is the saying of Ibn al-Ruqayyat:

Ancient glory, whose first founder
Reached ʿĀd, and before it Iram.

And similar to it is the saying of Zuhayr:

And other peoples, whose number the Madhi (a people) see,
Of the weaving of Dawud, or what Iram inherited.

Thus His saying, ﴿Iram﴾, is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to ʿĀd, to indicate that they are the first ʿĀd. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal). It is not declined (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf), because of its proper-name status (ʿalamiyya) and its feminine form, taking the tribe as the reference. ʿĀd is declined when the reference is the people (ḥayy). It may also be left undeclined when the reference is the tribe. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read it this way in one of the two reports from him, and he preferred declining it, because it is light, its middle letter being quiescent. Some scholars assumed an omitted noun (muḍāf) in the sentence, meaning "the tribe (sibṭ) of Iram," and made Iram the name of their mother. This view was reported by al-Fīrūzābādī in al-Qāmūs. The reason for not declining it is clear. Others insisted that it is the name of their grandfather. The meaning of their being his tribe is that they are the children of his son. On this view, the reason for not declining it does not appear, and perhaps this is what led some to make it the name of their mother. However, I have seen in the glosses of some scholars on the Iṣāmiyya super-commentary on the tafsir of al-Bayḍāwī that Iram is not declined whether it is the name of the tribe or of its ancestor, because of proper-name status and foreignness (ʿujma). He said that both features are also found in ʿĀd, but because it is triliteral with a quiescent middle, it may be either declined or not. He claimed this is the correct view. Mujāhid, Qatādah and Ibn Isḥāq said it is the name of the tribe. With this reading there is no need to assume an omitted noun.

Then His saying, ﴿dhāt al-ʿimād﴾, is an adjective of ﴿Iram﴾ itself. The intended meaning is "possessors of tall stature," comparing their statures to pillars (aʿmida). From this comes the expression "a man is muʿammad" or "ʿammadān" when he is tall. This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, and it is well known that the height of one of them was twelve cubits or more. In the tafsir of al-Kawāshī it is said: "They said: the height of the tallest of them was four hundred cubits, and one of them would take a great rock and turn it over upon the tribe, destroying them." This is reported from Qatādah and Ibn ʿAbbās in the report of ʿAṭāʾ. The intended meaning is "possessors of tents and pillars." They were nomads in spring, and when the vegetation grew they returned to their dwellings. Many others said: they were Bedouins, people of tent-poles and tents, which they inhabited while settled and while travelling. It was also said: the intended meaning is "possessors of high rank," or "possessors of dignity," or "possessors of firmness and long life." All of these are meant figuratively (ʿalā al-istiʿāra).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Which had not been created like them in the lands﴾ is another attribute of it; that is, no one like them had been created in greatness of physique and strength in the lands of the world. I have already heard what was transmitted from al-Kawashi a moment ago, and what was mentioned in it, that each of them was... etc. There has come in a marfu' hadith, narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'd Yakrib: "..." It has also been said: Iram is the name of a city belonging to them. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is Alexandria. Ibn al-Musayyib and al-Muqbiri said: it is Damascus. It has been said: it is the name of their land, which lies between Oman and Hadramawt, and it is a land of sand dunes and al-ahqaf (winding sand ridges). Indeed, He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And mention the brother of 'Ad, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf﴾. On this basis, the view that their city was Alexandria is objected to, and so is the view that it was Damascus, since neither of them is among the lands of al-Ahqaf and the sand dunes, unless it is said that what is meant here is the first 'Ad, while what is meant in the verse of al-Ahqaf is the later 'Ad, and this entails that their dwelling places were not the same. On the view that it is the name of their city or the name of their land, it is by way of an elided genitive construction to make the apposition correct; that is: the people of Iram. It has also been said: an elided noun is to be assumed on the side of the head noun; that is: "in the city or land of 'Ad, Iram," and this, as you see, is weak. The diptotic form (non-declension) is applied on both readings for the reason you have heard. Most scholars hold that it is the name of a great city in the land of Yemen, and the two attributes apply to it. The intended meaning is: the one with the lofty construction, or the one with the pillars, which had no equal in spaciousness and beauty of houses and gardens in the lands of the world. It is also narrated that 'Ad had two sons: Shaddad and Shadid. They ruled and subdued, then Shadid died and the matter passed to Shaddad, who ruled the world, and its kings submitted to him. He heard the mention of Paradise and said: "I will build the like of it." So he built Iram in some deserts of Aden over three hundred years, and his lifespan was nine hundred years. It is a great city whose palaces are of gold and silver and whose pillars are of chrysolite and ruby, and in it are kinds of trees and flowing rivers. When its construction was completed, he set out toward it with the people of his kingdom, and when they were a day and a night's journey away from it, God, exalted, sent upon them a cry from heaven, and they perished. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Qilabah that he went out seeking his camels, came upon it, and carried away whatever he could of what was there. His report reached Mu'awiyah, who summoned him and he related the matter to him. Mu'awiyah sent for Ka'b and asked him, and he said: "It is Iram of the pillars, and a man of the Muslims will enter it in your time, ruddy, fair-complexioned, short, with a mole on his eyebrow and a mole on his heel, who goes out seeking his camels." Then he turned and saw Ibn Qilabah and said: "By God, this is that man." As for the report of Shaddad mentioned, its transmission is similar in weakness; indeed its chain is not sound, as al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned, so it is fabricated, like the report of Ibn Qilabah.

It is related from Mujahid that Iram is a verbal noun of aram, yaram, meaning "to perish," so Iram means "destruction," in the accusative in the manner of the accusative of the figurative (comparative) verbal noun, in apposition to "dhat" (possessor of). And "allati" is an attribute of ﴿dhat al-'imad﴾, meaning the city, and "kayfa fa'ala" is in the sense of "kayfa ahlaka" (how He destroyed). It is as if it were said: "Have you not seen how your Lord destroyed 'Ad, like the destruction of the people of the pillars, which had no equal in the lands?" This is a strange view, not a close one. Al-Hasan read: "bi-'Adin Iram," with 'Ad in construct with Iram, so Iram may be a grandfather, with the two attributes applying to 'Ad, or it may be a city with the two attributes applying to it, and it is permitted that they apply to 'Ad. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "bi-'Adin Aramа," with the construct again, except that Aram is with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the ra'; it is said that this is a dialect form for the city only. From al-Dahhak it is related that he read "bi-'Ad" both diptotic and non-diptotic, and "Aram" with a fatha on the hamza and a sukun on the ra' for lightness, its original form being "Aram" like "fakhdh." It was also read: "Iram dhat," with Iram in construct with dhat; it is said that "Iram" is the name of a place, and the meaning is "'Ad, the markers of the people of the pillars, which is their city." And "allati" is an attribute of ﴿dhat al-'imad﴾ according to the more apparent view. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he read "Arrama" with shadda as a past verb, with dhat in the accusative as object; that is, God, exalted, made the possessors of pillars into dust (ramim); and "Arima" according to what is in al-Bahr is a substitute for a verb or an explanation of it. The intended meaning of "dhat al-'imad" here is either 'Ad itself, and there would be the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, whose point is evident; or their city, and "making it ramim" would mean its destruction, as a metaphor for making them so. Ibn al-Zubayr read "lam yakhluq" in the active voice, with its subject being the pronoun of the Mighty and Majestic, and "mithluha" in the accusative as object. From him also: "lam nakhluq" with the plural of majesty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 9:

﴿And Thamud﴾ is conjoined to (ʿAd). They were a well-known tribe, named after their forefather Thamud, brother of Judays. The two were sons of Abir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh (peace be upon him). They were Arabs of the al-ʿAariba (the original Arabs), dwelling in al-Hijr between the Hijaz and Tabuk, and they worshipped idols. The name is not declined (diptote) on account of its being a proper noun (ʿalamiyya) and its feminine form (taʾnith). Ibn Wathhab read it with tanwin, declining it by considering it as the name of a tribe (al-hayy); so they say. Its apparent sense is that it is Arabic, and this has been stated explicitly, so it is said: it is faʿwal from al-thamd, which is a small amount of water with no source; from it is said: "So-and-so is mathmud (depleted), the women have cut off the source of his water (thamadathu al-nisaʾ)," meaning they have cut off the source of his water through their excessive intercourse with him; and mathmud is also said of one upon whom beggars have increased until the source of his wealth is exhausted. Al-Raghib related that it is non-Arabic (ʿajami), and so it is not declined on account of being a proper noun and foreignness (ʿujma).

﴿Who hewed out the rock﴾ That is: they cut the rocks of the mountains and made dwellings in them, which they carved out of the rock, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you hew out houses from the mountains﴾. It is said: the first to carve stones, rocks and marble was Thamud, and they built a thousand and seven hundred cities, all of them of stone; but I do not think this construction is sound.

﴿In the valley﴾ This is the Wadi al-Qura. It is also read with the letter yaʾ (bi-l-wadi as "bi-l-wadi" variant reading), the bāʾ is for location (li-l-zarfiyya), and the prepositional phrase is related to "jabu" or to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject or the object. It is said: the bāʾ is for instrument (li-l-ala) or causation (li-l-sababiyya), related to "jabu"; that is: they hewed the rock in their valley or because of it, that is, they cut the rock, split it, and made it a valley and a place for their water, the deed of people of strength and hopes; and this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Whichever it is, the meaning of "jabu" is cutting, and its apparent sense is that it is literal in this; you say: "I traversed the lands (jubtu al-bilad ajuba-ha)" when you cross them. The poet said:

"Nor have I seen a she-camel before her who carried sixty wasq, nor traversed a land with her."

From this comes "al-jawab" (answer/reply), because it cuts off the question. Al-Raghib said: al-jawb is cutting the jawba, which is the open part of the land, and then it is used for cutting any land; and the answer of speech is what cuts the jawb so that it reaches from the mouth of the speaker to the hearing of the listener, but it is specific to speech that returns in reply, not to the initial address of discourse. End. So choose for yourself what is sweet to you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 10:

﴿And Pharaoh, the possessor of stakes﴾ He was described thus because of the multitude of his soldiers and their tents, the pegs of which they drive into the ground at their encampments. Or it is because he used to drive four stakes for the one being tortured, fastening him with them, stretched out flat on the ground, and then he would torture him with whatever he wished, by beating, burning, or otherwise. The discussion of this has already preceded.

Those who transgressed in the lands. This is either in the genitive, as an attribute of the previously mentioned ʿĀd and those after them, or in the accusative or nominative, as a term of censure. The meaning is that every transgressor among them transgressed in the lands. The same applies to His words, ﴿and they multiplied corruption therein﴾, meaning through disbelief and all other sins.

﴿So your Lord poured upon them﴾ means that He, glorified is He, sent down a severe punishment upon each group of those peoples, following what they had done of transgression and corruption.

﴿a scourge of punishment﴾ means a scourge of punishment. The construct here has the sense of "from" (min), and "punishment" means "that by which one is punished." What is meant is the various kinds of torment that befell each of them, which are explained in the other noble surahs. The word "sawt" (scourge) originally is a verbal noun from sāṭa, yasūṭu, meaning "to mix." The poet said:

O Ḥārith, if our blood were mixed,
they would separate until no blood touches blood.

The word then became common for the braided leather whip with which one strikes. It was named so either because its strands are mixed with one another, or because flesh is mixed with blood by it. The expression of sending it down as "pouring" indicates its abundance, continuity and persistence, since pouring is a figure for spilling something liquid, or something that flows like it, such as grains or sand, and emptying it out with force, abundance and continuity. Its attribution to the scourge, although, as you have heard, it is not of this kind, is based on likening the speed of its descent to a poured substance. As for calling what was sent down a "scourge," it has been said that this indicates that, despite its severity compared to what is prepared for them in the Hereafter, it is like a whip compared to all else with which one is punished. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that attributing the scourge to punishment is a reduction of what befell them from it, and the expression of pouring, which indicates abundance, does not contradict this, since few and many are relative matters.

It is also permitted that by "punishment" is meant "torment," and the construct then has the sense of "of" (the lām), while the matter of the expression "pouring" and the naming "scourge" is as explained above. The verse is of the kind of His words, ﴿so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger﴾ (16:112).

It is also permitted that the construct is like the construct in "lujayn al-mā'" (silver of water), meaning: so your Lord poured upon them a punishment like a scourge, in the sense of various kinds of punishment mixed with one another, as the strands of a whip are mixed with one another. It is also permitted that "scourge" is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, and the construct is like the construct in "jard qaṭīfa" (a cloak of cloth), meaning: so your Lord poured upon them a punishment that is "mesawwaṭ," that is, mixed. Its outcome is: He poured kinds of punishment, some of which were mixed with others.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ﴿scourge of punishment﴾ means "a portion of punishment," and it is said: its severity. This is because punishment may come by means of a whip. He meant that the purpose is depiction, and what is most fitting to the eloquence of the revelation is what has been mentioned above.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 89, verse 14:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in ambush.﴾ This is a justification (*ta'lil*) for what precedes it, and an announcement that the disbelievers of his people (ﷺ) will be struck by a punishment like that which befell their likes mentioned above. This is indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship (*rububiyya*) together with its attribution to his (ﷺ) pronoun. *Al-mirsad* is the place where the watchers (*al-rasad*) stand and lie in wait, and it is of the pattern *mif'al* from *rasadahu*, like *al-miqat* from *waqatahu*.

In the statement there is a metaphor by representation (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*), in which God's being a guardian of the deeds of the sinners, as is narrated from al-Dahhak, is likened to one who is watching them and will requite them for the smallest and the tiniest, so that none of them escapes from Him, glory be to Him, in the manner of one who sits on the road, lying in wait for whoever travels it in order to seize him and inflict upon him what he wills. Then the word for one of the two is applied to the other. On this view, the verse is a threat to the sinners in general. It has also been said that it is a threat to the disbelievers, and it has been said that it is a threat to the sinners and a promise to others, and this is the apparent meaning of the statement of al-Hasan; that is, He, glory be to Him, watches the deeds of the children of Adam.

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that *al-mirsad* be an intensive form (*sigha mubalagha*), like *al-mit'am* and *al-mit'an*. Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying that if it were as he claimed, the particle *ba'* (in *bi-l-mirsad*) would not enter it, because it is not in a position where it can be entered, neither as an extra particle (*za'ida*) nor as a non-extra one. It was answered that, on that view, the particle is abstractive (*tajridiyya*). Yes, it does entail applying the name *al-mirsad* to God, exalted and majestic is He, and there is something questionable in that.

[As for man] and so on: this is connected to what precedes it, as if it were said: He, glory be to Him, is ever watchful (labi-l-mirsad) concerning the Hereafter, so He, mighty and majestic, seeks only effort for it. As for man, he is concerned with nothing but this world and its pleasures. If he obtains some of it, he is pleased, and if not, he is angry. The fitting course would be that he be concerned only with what Allah, mighty and majestic, seeks, and that his state not be like this. It has also been said that it is connected to what precedes it and branches from it, in the sense that: man will inevitably be called to account, because he is between a destructive wealth that necessitates arrogance and boasting in the world, and a poverty he cannot bear, through which he disbelieves by impatience and by saying what is not fitting. But this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿When his Lord tests him﴾: that is, He treats him as one who tests him with wealth and ease, to see whether he will give thanks or not. The fa' in His words, glory be to Him, ﴿so He honours him and blesses him﴾ is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), for honouring and blessing are the very thing meant by the testing. Since honouring and blessing are in the same category, He limited Himself to His words ﴿honoured me﴾ in His words, glory be to Him, ﴿and he says, "My Lord has honoured me"﴾, and did not add "and blessed me" to it. This sentence is the predicate (khabar) of the subject, which is man, and the fa' is due to the meaning of the conditional and temporal sense in amma (as for). Idhan (then/when) is connected to "yaqulu" (says), and it is [Page 126] in the intention of postponement. The fa' is not prevented from this, as stated explicitly by al-Zamakhshari and others among the early grammarians, and those after them followed them, such as Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Safaqsi, along with a large group of exegetes. This, as al-Shihab said, is the truth from which there is no escape. But al-Radi and those who followed him, such as al-Badr al-Damamini in his commentary on the Mughni, disagreed with them. They said: the fronting of what follows the fa' over it is only permitted when the fronted element is the one separating amma from the fa', because of the purposes connected to fronting it. If there is another separating element, fronting something else is prohibited. Thus "amma Zayd ta'amaka fa-akil" is prohibited, though "amma ta'amuka fa-Zayd akil" is permitted. They said, regarding this, that since they were obliged to delete the conditional, it would follow that its particle would fall upon the fa' of the response, which is disliked, so necessity called for a separation between them by something from what follows the fa', and a single separating element suffices, so it is obligatory to limit oneself to it. Al-Jalbi, the annotator of the Mutawwal, claimed that this is agreed upon, and he refuted the exegetes' earlier parsing with it, saying: it is an error. The correct view is that the temporal adverbial be considered attached to an implied element, which in reality is "ibtada'" (began), and the sense is: "As for the matter of man when..." and so on. So the temporal adverbial is part of the separated component and is not a second separating element in it, like your saying: "As for the kindness of Zayd to the poor is good." He means by this estimate that it is not valid for the sentence "yaqulu" to occur as a predicate of the matter, except by strained interpretation, such as the verb being taken as a verbal noun (masdar), even if "an" (the verbal particle) is not present with it in the wording, as is said in: "You hear of the Mu'ayyidi that he is better than that you see him." And this is an escape from the cloud to the gutter.

Abu al-Baqa' went to the view that "idha" is conditional, and His words, ﴿and he says﴾, are its response, and the conditional sentence is the predicate of "al-insan" (man). This entails the deletion of the fa' without "qawl" (saying), and it has been said that this is a necessity (darurah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 16:

The saying of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿But as for man, when his Lord tries him⁠﻿ by providing for him,⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿ ﴾ [He treats him as one who tries and tests him with need and poverty, to see whether he will be patient or not].

﴿...and so restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me!"﴾ [The implied sense: "As for him, that is, man, when He tries him..." etc., so that the division is valid and the balance is complete. The rest of the discussion here is as in the previous verse. It is apparent that both clauses include a refutation of the saying of man that they contain: and the denial of his saying, when his provision is restricted, "My Lord has humiliated me!" because it indicates the shortness of his outlook and the badness of his thinking, in that he supposed that the restriction of provision is humiliation, although it may lead to the honour of both abodes. And because it is not humiliation at all, the Most High did not say, in explaining the trial, "so He humiliated him," but rather "and restricts his provision," in parallel with what He said first: ﴿...then He honours him and blesses him﴾. And the denial of his saying, "When my Lord honours me, He honours me," alongside the Most High's saying "then He honours him" at first, is because he affirmed God's honouring of him in a way contrary to what God affirmed; namely, the intention that God gave him what He gave him as an honour he deserved and merited, in keeping with their pride and their claim to the nobility of their ranks. The summary is that the one who denies it being due to merit of lineage or descent is, in the detailed statement, what indicates that the very basis of honour is denied, not merely that it is due to merit; and the denial of the very basis of humiliation supports this. The reason the honour God affirmed is apparent is that the Exalted and Majestic affirmed honour through the granting of wealth and expansion, which is making it a general honour establishing nearness to Him; so He denied that he had any share of that honour. It is also permitted that the denial is only of humiliation; meaning, when he is favoured with good and honoured by it, he acknowledges God's favour and honour; and when he is not favoured, he calls the withholding of favour disgrace, and it is not so. This is supported by the mention of honour in the saying of the Most High: ﴿then He honours him﴾. In the verse together with what follows there is a hint of the style of the Most High's saying: ﴿Indeed, man was created anxious; when evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾. It is not hidden that the first aspect is the correct one.

Ibn Kathir read "akramani" and "ahanani" with the yā' affirmed in both; Nafi' affirmed it in pausal and continuous recitation and omitted it in pause; Abu 'Amr allowed both options; the rest of the seven omitted it in both continuous recitation and pause. Whoever omits it in pause pronounces the nun with sukun there. Abu Ja'far, 'Isa, Khalid, al-Hasan (with a variant reported from him), and Ibn 'Amir read "faqaddara" with the dal doubled, for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 89, verses 17–19:

﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke to man for his two stated sayings, and a denial of them both, not of the last one alone as in the final interpretation. Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) explicitly stated what we have said. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is: "I did not test him with wealth because of his honour with Me, nor did I test him with poverty because of his humiliation before Me; rather, that is purely by divine decree and destiny (al-qada' wal-qadar)."
Page 127
His words, glorified be He: ﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾ and so on, are a transition and an escalation from condemning him for ugly speech to condemning him for the uglier deed, and the turn to direct address serves to intensify the reproach and emphasize the censure.

It has also been said that this is with the implied verb "say" (qul), so there is no turn of address. Yet in it there is an indication of belittling them, along with what that contains. The plural is used in view of the meaning of "man" (al-insan), since the intended sense is the species. That is: "Rather, you have deeds and states that are worse than what has been mentioned, and more indicative of your greed for wealth, since Allah the Exalted honours you with abundant wealth, yet you do not fulfil what is obligatory upon you regarding it, namely honouring the orphan through kindness to him and benevolence toward him."

In a hadith: "The dearest of houses to Allah the Exalted is a house in which there is an honoured orphan."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Jahdari and Abu 'Amr read ﴿do not honour﴾ (*la yukrimun*) with the third-person plural (ya' of absence).

﴿And you do not urge one another﴾ (*wa la tahaddun*), with one of the two taa's of *tatahaddun* removed, meaning: "and [they] do not urge or incite one another ﴿to feed the poor﴾," that is, to feed him. Thus *ta'am* (food) is a verbal noun meaning the act of feeding, like *'ata'* (giving) meaning the act of giving.

Abu Hayyan claimed that it is better to take it to mean the food itself, with an omitted noun, so that the meaning is "on giving away the food of the poor." The word *miskin* (poor) is taken to include the destitute (*faqir*). 'Abdullah, 'Alqamah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak and al-Shirazi, from al-Kisa'i, read it like the common reading, except that they vowelled the taa' of *tuhaddun* (you urge) as from *muhaddah* (urging). Abu 'Amr, and those I have heard from al-Hasan and those with him, read ﴿do not urge﴾ (*la yahuddun*) with the third-person ya' and no alif after the ha'; the rest of the seven read it with the second-person taa' in the same way, and likewise the two verbs following. The verb in both readings may be understood as transitive with an omitted object: some said "themselves" or "yourselves," some said "their families" or "your families," and some said "anyone." It is also permitted, and this is the better view, that it be treated as intransitive for generality.

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾ (*al-turath*), that is, the inheritance; its root is *wurath*, and the waw was replaced with a taa', as in *tukhmah* and *tuklah* and similar words.

﴿Devouring greedily﴾ (*aklan lamman*), that is, "with *lamm*" (gathering), or it is itself *lamm* by way of emphasis. *Lamm* means gathering together, and from it is the saying of al-Nabighah:

"I am not one who would leave behind a brother whom he does not gather in spite of his faults, whoever are the most refined of men."

Here it means combining the lawful and the unlawful, and what is praised and what is not praised. From it is also the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

"When the one who has *lamm* is followed by blame, may the Merciful not sanctify those grinding stones."

He means: you combine in your eating your share of the inheritance and the share of others. It is related that they did not give inheritance to women or to young children, so they would consume their portion, and they would say: "None takes inheritance except one who fights and protects the territory." Yet they knew from the sharia of Isma'il, peace be upon him, that they inherit; and thus the objection is dispelled that the surah is Meccan and the verse on inheritance is Medinan, and that lawfulness and unlawfulness are known only from the revealed law, since the rational good and evil (*al-husn wal-qubh al-'aqliyyan*) are not our school of thought.

It has also been said: it means that you eat what the deceased, whose inheritance it is, gathered from both lawful and unlawful sources, knowing this, so you combine in eating between its lawful and its unlawful parts.

In the *Kashshaf*: it is possible that the heir who gained the wealth easily and calmly, without his brow sweating over it, be blamed for spending extravagantly and eating it lavishly, combining every kind of desirable food, drink, fruit and the like, as false heirs do. It has been criticized as not fitting the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 89, verses 17–19:

The verb in both readings may be understood as transitive with an omitted object: some said "themselves" or "yourselves," some said "their families" or "your families," and some said "anyone." It is also permitted, and this is the better view, that it be treated as intransitive for generality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 22:

﴿And your Lord comes﴾. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is that He, glorified is He, manifests Himself to the creation at that time, and this is not a coming in the sense of moving from one place to another, and likewise is the coming of the Great Calamity (al-Tamma) and the Deafening Blast (al-Sakhkha). It has also been said: the statement is elliptical, with an omitted noun (al-mudaf, i.e. a word omitted before a genitive), for the sake of emphasizing the terror, meaning: the command of your Lord and His decree, glorified is He, comes. A group of scholars chose that it is a figurative expression (tamthil) for the manifestation of the signs of His power, exalted is He, and the clear display of the effects of His might and His authority, mighty is His authority. His state, glorified is He, in that matter has been likened to the state of a king who comes in person, so that there appear to those present before him, from the effects of awe and governance, what does not appear when his armies, viziers and close associates are present, all of them together. You know what the early generation (al-salaf) said about the ambiguous (al-mutashabih) statements. ﴿And the angel﴾, i.e. the category of angels, so it includes the angels of the heavens, peace be upon them, all of them, ﴿rank upon rank﴾, i.e. standing in rows, or possessing ranks. It has been said that on the Day of Resurrection the angels of each heaven will descend, and they will stand in rows, one row after another, according to their stations and levels, encircling the jinn and humankind. It has been said: they will stand according to the places of the affairs connected with them, and this is close to what has been mentioned. It is also narrated that the angels of each heaven will be a row around the earth, so the rows will be seven, according to what is apparent. Some of the eminent scholars said: the apparent meaning is that "the angel" is more general than the angels of the heavens and others, its definiteness is for comprehensiveness (li'l-istighraq), and it was claimed that their standing in rows according to their levels is like the standing of the people of this world in prayer. Its apparent meaning is that it is a standing in rows without encircling. I have seen no report indicating that they stand encircling.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 23:

﴿And Hell will be brought forth on that Day﴾. It has been said: this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Hellfire will be made manifest to those who see﴾, on the basis that its "bringing" is a metaphorical expression for its being made apparent. It has been preferred that it is meant literally.

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand reins, with each rein held by seventy thousand angels who will drag it." "And in another narration with an addition: 'until it is placed to the left of the Throne, and it has rage and roaring.'"

And it has come in some reports: "That Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and conferred with him privately, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood for the prayer with his gaze lowered, so 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) asked him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Jibril (peace be upon him) brought me this verse: ﴿No! When the earth is pounded to powder﴾ ... to the end of the verse.' 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said to him: 'How will it be brought?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It will be led by seventy thousand reins, each rein led by seventy thousand angels. While they are thus, it will suddenly break loose from them and escape from their hands. Had they not caught up with it and seized it, it would have burned everyone gathered.'"

And in another narration: "Had Allah, exalted is He, not restrained it, it would have burned the heavens and the earth."

The interpretation of all that has been mentioned and similar things that have been reported, and taking it as figurative, is called for only by the impossibility of the movement that literal "bringing" to Hell would entail; but by my life, this is not impossible. So it is permissible that it come out and move from its place at the gathering, then return to it, and the state on that Day is beyond what minds imagine.

﴿On that Day﴾ is a substitute for ﴿when the earth is pounded﴾. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words is that the governing element for it is the same governing element as in the substituted term, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿man will remember﴾. This view has been attributed to Sibawayh. In al-Bahr it is said: the well-known view is otherwise, namely that the substitution is on the intention of repeating the governing element; and what is apparent to me is the first view. "Yatadhakkaru" (will remember) is from dhikr, the opposite of forgetting; that is: man will remember what he neglected in its details, by witnessing its traces and its rulings, or by Allah's bringing it to his mind and causing it to occur to him even if he has not yet witnessed a trace, or by seeing it with his own eye, on the basis that deeds take on bodily form in the next creation, appearing in forms befitting them, good or ugly; or from remembrance in the sense of admonition; that is: he will be admonished by what he sees of the signs of the power of Allah, mighty and majestic, and the greatness of His majesty and dignity, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how can the remembrance be for him?﴾ is a parenthetical clause brought to establish that it is not truly remembrance, since it is devoid of benefit because it does not occur at its proper time. ("Anna") is a predicate placed first, and ("al-dhikra") is the subject, and ("lahu") is connected to what the predicate is connected to; that is: and from where would remembrance be for him when its time has passed? It has been said: there is an omitted genitive construction there; that is: and how for him is the benefit of remembrance? It must be estimated so that there is no contradiction. You have known that this is achieved by what was established earlier, and that if the particularity of the lam is taken as restricted to the beneficial, the meaning is sound without estimation, and the denial becomes that remembrance is for him and not against him. As for its being a report of what he used to be in the world, of lack of heed and admonition, this is nothing.

The verse has been used as evidence that repentance, as such, is not necessarily acceptable by reason, as the Mu'tazila claimed on the basis of their doctrine that what is most beneficial (al-aslah) is obligatory for Allah. It has been said in its explanation: if its acceptance were obligatory, then the acceptance of this remembrance would be obligatory, for it is repentance; since repentance, as explained in its proper place, is regret for sin as sin, and resolve not to return to it when one is able, and no one has included in its definition that it occurs in this world, though the beneficial repentance can only occur in it. And this remembrance is the very regret mentioned. Al-Dahhak has explicitly stated, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, that it is repentance but it was not accepted because the benefit that is among the necessary consequences of acceptance does not follow from it. It was objected that the Mu'tazila only say that its acceptance is obligatory on condition that the obligations have not been lifted. It has also been said: his remembrance is not part of repentance at all, for he knows that repentance occurs only in this world, as his saying, exalted is He, indicates:

﴿He will say: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ And what is in it of the inference (istidlal) that has preceded is to be understood, so do not be heedless.

This clause is either a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion, a grammatical apposition) for "yatadhakkaru" (he remembers), or a *istinaf* (resumptive clause) that answers a question arising from it, as if it were said: "What does he say when he remembers?" So it was said: "He says: 'Oh, I wish I had...'" The *lam* is *lam al-ta'lil* (the lam of causation). The intended meaning of "his life" is his life in the Hereafter. The object of "qaddamtu" (I sent forth) is omitted, so it is as if he said: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth, for the sake of this life of mine, righteous deeds by which I would benefit in it." It has also been said: the lam is the lam of causation, but the meaning is: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth righteous deeds for the sake of living a beneficial life." He said that because he will neither die nor live at that time, and this is, as you see, far-fetched.

It is permissible that the lam be *lam tawqitiyya* (the lam of time), like it is in such phrases as: "I wrote it for the fifteenth night that passed of Muharram," and "I came at sunrise." The intended meaning of "his life" is then his life in this world; that is: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth and performed righteous deeds during my life in this world, so that I might benefit from them today." There is no trace in this wish of an indication that the servant is independent (*istiqlal*) in his action. It only indicates the belief that he was able to send forth righteous deeds. As for whether that is by the sheer power of Allah the Exalted, or by the creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He diverts the acquiring power (*qudra kasiba*) toward him, then no. Al-Zamakhshari claimed it to be a proof of independence and used it to refute the *Mujbira* (Determinists), whom in his view are not the Mu'tazila, supposing that the wish and the restriction (*hajr*) are incompatible. You know that there is no indication of that. In *al-Kashf* it is stated that wishing may occur regarding the impossible, since in that state he is like one drowning. Moreover, the People of the Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) do not say that free choice (*ikhtiyar*) is wholly negated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verse 25–26:

﴿فَيَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ That is, on the day when what has been mentioned of states and statements occurs. ﴿لا يُعَذِّبُ عَذابَهُ أحَدٌ﴾ ﴿ولا يُوثِقُ وثاقَهُ أحَدٌ﴾ The pronoun (al-ha') may refer to Allah, ʿazza wa-jall; that is, none other than Him, ʿazza wa-jall, takes charge of the punishment of Allah the Exalted and His bonds, glorified is He. It is as if it were said: none performs the punishment of Allah the Exalted and His bonds, nor directly carries them out. This is because the verb (al-fiʿl) is included within every specific act, and this usage is common, as in:

"And indeed the caravan and the leaping have been made to separate." And if we do not think but a [mere] thought, then ʿadhab (punishment) is the object, and likewise wathaq (bonds). In this there is the magnification of the punishment of Allah the Exalted and His bonds, glorified is He, upon this human being whose states He has described, by way of kinaya (allusion). As for what Ibn al-Hajib claimed, that the meaning is weak if the pronoun returns to Him, the Exalted, on the basis that the magnification required by the context is lost due to heedlessness of the subtle point of the kinaya, [this is not so].

Or the pronoun may refer to the described human being, and the idafa is to the object; that is: none of the guardians (al-zabaniya) punishes or binds any one of the people of the Fire in the manner in which they punish and bind him. It is as if he is the most severe of them in punishment and bonds, because he is the most severe of them in evil deeds and vile states. This is a good interpretation, indeed it is more preferable than the first, as we shall indicate, if Allah the Exalted wills.

And Ibn Sirin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Bahriyya, Sallam, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, Sahl, and Kharija (from Abu ʿAmr) read: «لا يُعَذَّبُ» and «ولا يُوثَقُ» in the passive voice. Then the pronoun in ʿadhabahu and wathaqahu refers to the described human being; that is: none is punished like his punishment, and none is bound with chains and shackles like his bonds, because of his extremity in disbelief and opposition. The word ʿadhab is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), standing in the place of taʿdhib (punishment); either because in origin it has its meaning, like salam meaning taslim (greeting), and then it was transferred to that by which one is punished, or because it is placed in its position, just as ʿata' (gift) is placed in the position of iʿta' (giving). Likewise wathaq. It is also permitted that the meaning be: none bears the punishment of the human being, nor is his bond tied by anyone, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ولا تَزِرُ وازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرى﴾ (and no bearer shall bear the burden of another). The punishment on him is taken in its common sense, and the accusative is by way of implying the meaning of tahmil (bearing) in taʿdhib (punishment). The first is more fitting to the context of severity upon this human being who was negligent during the time of his capacity, and the second interpretation of the first reading corresponds to this, as is not hidden. What is meant by "none is punished like his punishment" is that none of his kind is punished like him, such as the disobedient ones of that kind; thus it does not necessarily follow that he is more severely punished than Iblis and those of his rank. Furthermore, the apparent meaning is that what is intended is the category of those characterized by what has been mentioned. It has been said that what is intended is Umayya ibn Khalaf, and it was said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning, even if it is said that the verse was revealed concerning those mentioned. As for the view that this bound punishment refers to Iblis, may God's curse be upon him, it is nothing; since he is not called a human being (insan), and the pronoun's referring to him, even though no mention of him has preceded, rather than to the human being mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَذَكَّرُ الإنْسانُ﴾ etc., is something that should not be given any attention.

And Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' (with a variant from him) read: «وِثاقَهُ» with a kasra on the waw.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning is that what is intended is the category of those characterized by what has been mentioned. And Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' (with a variant from him) read: «وِثاقَهُ» with a kasra on the waw.

This is a description of the condition of one who finds rest in the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and in obedience to Him, following on from the description of one who found rest in this world and settled in it. It has been mentioned that this is in the sense of speech, meaning: Allah the Exalted says, ﴿O soul﴾ and so on, either directly, as He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him, or through an angel. It has been inferred that this speech occurs at the completion of the reckoning.

When it reaches Him, the Mighty and Majestic, it finds rest and becomes independent, through Him, the Glorified, of its own existence and all its affairs, and turns to nothing other than Him, the Majestic and Exalted, entirely.

This is a good view, and the connection according to it is that this soul is the one that admonishes and remembers, in contrast to the human being described previously, for remembrance is in proportion to the strength of certainty. Do you not see His words, the Exalted: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾?

It has also been said that it is the secure soul, which neither fear nor grief will disturb on the Day of Resurrection, namely the believing soul today, which dies in faith. It has been said that there is a rationale for this by analogy: just as it is not inflected for the dual or plural in addressing a dual or plural, so it is not made feminine when addressing a feminine. And treating "nafs" here as masculine and then as feminine is something the soul at peace does not pay attention to.

﴿ارْجِعِي﴾ That is: from the place where you were reckoned.

This is because the blessed (al-su'ada') have, before the reckoning (hisab), as is understood from the reports, a special station in the place of gathering (al-mahshar) where Allah, may He be exalted, honours them. In it they do not find the weariness that others find in their stations. From it, one after another is called to the reckoning. So when this statement is made at the completion of the reckoning,
صفحة 131
its meaning must be what has been mentioned. It is also possible that the meaning is: return with the heart emptied of deeds, of turning toward them, and of concern over whether they will be accepted or not. That is, return to contemplating {your Lord} and to devotion to Him, and to abandoning attention to anything other than Him, may He be mighty and majestic, as you were at first.
