**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 89, verses 29–30:**

﴿So enter among My servants﴾, into the company of My righteous servants who are sincere to Me, be strung on their thread, and be among their number.

﴿And enter My Garden﴾. It is coordinated (ʿatf) with the sentence before it, and it falls under the scope of the particle fa' (then), which indicates that what follows comes immediately after what precedes, without delay. It seems that the command to enter the company of Allah's righteous servants indicates spiritual happiness, because the soul is fully at ease with a righteous companion. The command to enter the Garden indicates bodily happiness. Because the first is superior to the second, the first command was placed first and the second was introduced as a completion (tatmim). The subtle point in the shift of address (iltifat) in both is clear with slight reflection.

The verb "entered" (al-dukhul) takes fi (in) the first time and is used without it the second time. Abu Hayyan said: "Because the thing entered into, if it is not a true place (zarf haqiqi), is in usage followed by fi. You say: 'I entered into the matter' (dakhaltu fi al-amr) and 'I entered into the crowd of people' (dakhaltu fi ghimar al-nas). But if it is a true place, it is in most cases followed directly without the intermediary of fi. So do not be unmindful." 

It has also been said: the meaning is "return to the promise of your Lord." It has been inferred (istuzhira) that, on the supposition that this statement comes after the completion of the reckoning, the promise of Allah the Exalted meant is the Garden and being with His righteous servants, and that fa' is explanatory (tafsiriyyah). This interpretation faces a difficulty regarding the command to return, since it requires that the Garden be a place of rest for the soul before that. It was answered that this requirement is realized on the basis that the soul existed potentially in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, when he was in the Garden. Something similar has been said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an for you will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ (28:85), according to what has been related from Amir al-Mu'minin Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the "place of return" meant is the Garden and not Mecca.

You should know that this, despite what is in it, is not complete except on the view that the Garden of Adam, peace be upon him, is the same Garden that the believers will enter on the Day of Resurrection, not another garden that existed on earth. The disagreement on this is strong, as is not hidden from one who has consulted the book Miftah al-Sa'adah (Key to Happiness) by the scholar Ibn al-Qayyim and examined the proofs of both sides.

It has also been said: the meaning is "return to the command of your Lord." It has been inferred that on this supposition the command (amr) means one of the affairs (uʾmur), and it is explained as Allah's dealing with her in a way that contains nothing that troubles her mind, or by distinguishing her with a noble station, or something similar, by which what the apparent sense of "return" requires is realized.

It has also been said: the meaning is "return to the honour of your Lord," meaning the kind of His honour, and "return" to Him is understood in terms of her honour being after death in the barzakh (the intermediate realm) or after resurrection and before the reckoning in some form of it. On this view, fa' is also said to be explanatory.

It is related from Ikrimah and al-Dahhak that this statement is made at the resurrection. It has been said that nafs (soul) also means the essence (dhat), that "Lord" refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that the speech contains an elided modifier. The place of His honour, the Exalted, cannot be estimated as meaning the specific station, as you have heard, because it will belong to her only afterwards.

It has been said: nafs means the spirit (rooh), and "Lord" means the Companion (al-Sahib). It has been explained as the body, and the rest of the verse remains as it is. That is: return to your body as you were in the world, then after returning to it enter among My servants and enter the abode of My reward.

It has also been said: the meaning of the soul and the Lord is as mentioned, and His saying ﴿among My servants﴾ contains an elided modifier, i.e., enter into the bodies of My servants. This was reported in a narration from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. The singular in the first and the plural in the second do no harm, because the meaning is generic.

Ibn Zayd and a group said that this statement is made at death, and this was supported by what Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah transmitted from Ibn Jubayr, who said: "It was recited in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿O soul at peace﴾ up to the end of the verse. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Indeed this is beautiful.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the angel will say it to you at death.'" Something similar came from the narration of al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, through the route of Thabit ibn Ajlan from Sulaym ibn Amir from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

According to this view, nafs means the spirit, and the meaning, as has been said, is: return by death to the sacred world of your Lord, content with what you are given of bliss, or pleased with your Lord and pleasing to Him, the Exalted. Then enter among the company of My close servants, dwellers of the sacred enclosures, and enter My Garden which I have prepared for those with souls at peace. These two entries follow the return, except that the first entry follows it without delay before the Day of Resurrection, and the second follows it with delay, because it is on the Day of Resurrection, if by entering the Garden is meant entering it in the mode of eternity. However, since the command is certain to be realized, it is permissible for it to be connected with fa'. It is also permissible that both commands be connected in this pattern if by entering among His servants is meant being strung among the righteous and sincere servants of their kind. On the supposition of this connection, it is permissible that it means "enter into the bodies of My servants." It is also permissible that the two commands be connected without delay if by entering among the servants is meant entering the company of those brought near, among the dwellers of the sacred enclosures, and by entering the Garden is meant entering it not in the mode of eternity but for a kind of enjoyment until the Hour comes. Thus in the hadith: "The spirits of believers are in the crops of green birds in the Garden."

In some reports: "When a believer dies, he is given half of the Garden." That is, half of his Garden which he was promised to enter on the Day of Resurrection. It has been mentioned as a reason for its being entered together with the sacred spirits, like polished mirrors: when some of them join others, the rays of the lights of knowledge reflect, so that each one appears with what completes it, and this becomes a cause for the completion of felicities and the magnification of ranks. But this, in my view, is a rhetorical statement (kalam khatabi). Some of the early generations (salaf) have said something that supports some of these aspects.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Salih that he said regarding the verse ﴿Return to your Lord﴾: "This is a sign of death, and her return to her Lord is her departure from the world. When the Day of Resurrection comes, it is said to her: 'Enter among My servants and enter My Garden.'" It has also been said that this statement is after death and before the Resurrection, and that the meaning of her return to her Lord is her return to her body for the questioning by the two angels. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said regarding the verse: "When the believer dies, his dwelling in the Garden is shown to him, and Blessed and Exalted says: 'O soul at peace, return to My presence, to your body from which you departed, content with what you have seen of My reward, and well-pleasing to Me, until Munkar and Nakir question you.'" It has been said that this is in three stations.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said regarding the verse: "She is given good news of the Garden at death, at resurrection, and on the Day of Gathering." It can be interpreted in accordance with what applies to all of them. It has also been said that this may be at all times of the soul in its worldly life, and that the command to return to the Lord means the command to return to Him in every matter of affairs, and the command to enter among the servants means the command to enter the company of the pure servants who have no authority of Satan over them, through increasing righteous deeds. The command to enter the Garden means the command to enter it by a near potential, so that after He, the Majestic and Exalted, had exceeded in describing the evil state of the commanding soul (al-ammarah) and warning against it, He addressed the soul at peace with this, and guided it to what would bring its righteousness and salvation. What is in this is not hidden, so it should not be counted as one of the aspects. Whichever of these aspects is taken, the apparent sense is their generality.

Even though Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the route of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, when he bought the well of Rumah and made it a water source for the people. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and it has been said that it was revealed concerning Khubayb ibn Adi, whom the people of Mecca crucified and turned his face toward Medina, and he said: "O Allah, if there is any good for me with You, turn my face toward Your qiblah." So Allah turned his face toward it, and no one afterwards was able to turn it. Thus, explaining the soul mentioned as one of these mentioned persons, as has been transmitted from some, is by way of illustration (tamthil), and the case of the cause is one of certain entry. The statement of Ibn Abbas about that soul, as Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, that it is the Prophet (ﷺ), should be understood in a similar way.

Some aspects of the verse indicate that souls were created before bodies and that their dwelling at that time was in the realm of malakut (the unseen dominion). The disagreement on this question is well known. The majority of theologians hold that souls are created when bodies are prepared for them, and so too did Plato and his followers.

Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Abu Ja'far, Abu Salih, Abu Shaykh, and al-Yamani read "ʿabdī" (My servant) in the singular. It has been inferred that the meaning is the genus, as with "nafs" (soul).

The Sufi masters, may their souls be sanctified, have a lengthy discourse on dividing the stations of the soul. They said that the verse includes three stations, among them the soul at peace (al-mutma'innah), the soul well-pleased (al-radiyyah), and the soul well-pleasing (al-mardiyyah). They explained each of them in the way they explained it. Whoever wants that should refer to their books. As for me, I say what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught one of the Companions, as Al-Tabarani and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Allah, I ask You for a soul at peace, that believes in meeting You, is content with Your decree, and is satisfied with Your gift."

The disagreement on this question is well known. The majority of theologians hold that souls are created when bodies are prepared for them, and so too did Plato and his followers.

Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Abu Ja'far, Abu Salih, Abu Shaykh, and al-Yamani read "ʿabdī" (My servant) in the singular. It has been inferred that the meaning is the genus, as with "nafs" (soul).

The Sufi masters, may their souls be sanctified, have a lengthy discourse on dividing the stations of the soul. They said that the verse includes three stations, among them the soul at peace (al-mutma'innah), the soul well-pleased (al-radiyyah), and the soul well-pleasing (al-mardiyyah). They explained each of them in the way they explained it. Whoever wants that should refer to their books. As for me, I say what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught one of the Companions, as Al-Tabarani and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Allah, I ask You for a soul at peace, that believes in meeting You, is content with Your decree, and is satisfied with Your gift."
